cases.difficulty_explanation: L1 — clean DFU case, all evidence present, front-page Dx matches indication

patient.name: Jerry Smith

radiology.finding: Positive for osteomyelitis and abscess

patient.clinical_notes: The patient presents with a right foot ulcer. The wound has been present since prior to debridement on 01/07/2025 and I&D on 01/19/2025. The patient has multiple comorbidities, including Type 2 Diabetes, CHF, COPD, and a history of MI. The wound was previously confirmed to have osteomyelitis and an abscess on X-ray dated 02/15/2025. The patient is currently managed with a total contact cast and hydrocolloid dressing. He remains on Amoxicillin for infection management, and his diabetes is controlled with insulin.

wagner_3_or_higher.evidence: X-Ray 02/15/2025 positive for osteomyelitis and abscess

no_measurable_healing.evidence: Wound 3.0 cm² on 01/07/25 to 2.8 cm² on 03/20/25 = minimal/no healing over 2+ months

cases.teaching_moment: Clean DFU presentation. Patient has Type 2 diabetes, Wagner Grade III confirmed by positive radiology for osteomyelitis, 30+ days of documented standard wound care with measurable lack of healing, and every required supporting element documented. This is what a textbook DFU referral looks like — recognize the pattern so you can spot deviations in harder cases.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L1 — clean ORN case, all radiation documentation present, front-page Dx matches indication

patient.name: Sean Black

radiology.finding: Positive for osteomyelitis

patient.clinical_notes: Osteoradionecrosis of the Mandible following 6500 cGy radiation therapy with pain, Xerostomia, Dysphagia, and exposed bone.

cases.teaching_moment: Textbook ORN case. The chart documents all four required elements: radiation amount (6500 cGy, well above the 4000 cGy minimum), anatomical location (mandible), end date of treatment (08/01/2020 — over 4 years ago, well past the typical 4-month wait), and clear signs/symptoms of injury (pain, xerostomia, dysphagia, exposed bone). Note: HBOT is NOT approved for dental extractions in a radiated field, but IS approved for these signs/symptoms of ORN.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L2 — 'Arthritis' listed first in Dx is the misdirection. Real indication is CROM, which appears second in the Dx list and is confirmed by imaging + treatment history.

patient.name: Sharron White

radiology.study: X-Ray and MRI of left knee
radiology.finding: Positive for osteomyelitis
Positive for osteomyelitis (persistent)

patient.clinical_notes: Recent MRI of the left knee (01/15/2025 and 03/11/2025) confirmed persistent osteomyelitis. The patient reports ongoing pain and stiffness in the left knee, with occasional edema.

prior_osteomyelitis_same_location.evidence: MRI 01/15/2025 positive for osteomyelitis in left knee

confirming_radiology_pathology_lab.evidence: MRI 03/11/2025 positive for persistent osteomyelitis (same location)

cases.teaching_moment: Don't stop at the front-page diagnosis. Arthritis is listed first, but the second diagnosis — Chronic Refractory Osteomyelitis — is the HBOT indication. Two MRIs months apart both confirm osteomyelitis in the same location (left knee), the patient has been on Vancomycin and underwent bone debridement, and the infection persists. That's CROM by definition: prior osteomyelitis in the same location, confirming imaging, and documented antibiotic + surgical management that has failed to resolve the infection. Scan ALL listed diagnoses on every chart before committing.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L2 — Patient has diabetes + had a foot wound — DFU is the obvious trap. But the real indication is Compromised Flap (failing post-BKA tissue flap). Multiple distractors point at DFU.

patient.name: Abigail Jones

radiology.finding: Edema and arterial stenosis

patient.wound_dressing: Silver Dressing and Collagen Matrix Dressing
patient.clinical_notes: This is a 70-year-old female with history significant for type II diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, and lower extremity occlusive arterial disease. Prior to amputation she underwent atherectomy with stent placement in the right lower extremity. Despite the revascularization efforts, the patient demonstrated gradual necrosis of the amputation's plantar tissue flap with dehiscence of the surgical incision and advancing cellulitis. She was at risk for complete failure of the tissue flap which was dusky and cyanotic.

graft_compromised.evidence: Tissue flap dusky and cyanotic, necrosis, dehiscence, advancing cellulitis

cases.teaching_moment: The diabetes and a previous foot wound are real, but they're not the indication. The patient just had a BKA on 03/01/2025, and the post-surgical tissue flap is failing — dusky, cyanotic, dehiscing, with advancing cellulitis. That's a Compromised Flap case, screened under the Compromised Grafts/Flaps indication, not DFU. The TCOM PO2 of 27 mmHg supports flap hypoxia (a Compromised Graft criterion), not DFU vascular assessment. Lesson: when a patient has multiple comorbidities AND a recent surgical procedure with a failing post-surgical flap, lead with the failing flap — not the comorbidities.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L3 — Disqualifier. Patient has diabetes + foot wound, but wound is Wagner Grade 2 (no osteo, no abscess, no positive culture). Does not meet DFU criteria.

patient.name: Harold Vance

radiology.finding: No osteomyelitis. No abscess. Soft tissue swelling only.

patient.clinical_notes: Patient presents for follow-up of a diabetic foot ulcer on the right plantar surface, present for approximately 6 weeks. Wound extends through the dermis but does not involve muscle, ligament, or bone on imaging. No clinical signs of deep infection or abscess. Wound culture from 03/01/2026 returned light growth of Staphylococcus epidermidis, likely skin contamination. Continuing standard wound care with hydrogel and diabetic shoes for offloading.

cases.teaching_moment: This patient does not qualify for HBOT under DFU. The wound is Wagner Grade 2 (extends through dermis but not into deeper tissues), with X-ray showing no osteomyelitis and no abscess. The 'positive' wound culture is light growth of Staph epidermidis — typical skin contamination, not the moderate-to-heavy growth on a deep wound that Wagner Grade 3 requires. DFU coverage requires Wagner Grade III or higher: deep wound with EITHER positive radiology for osteomyelitis/abscess OR positive deep wound culture showing moderate-to-heavy growth. This patient meets neither. Recommendation: continue standard wound care, re-evaluate if condition deteriorates or imaging changes.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L3 — Disqualifier. Patient with diabetes and wound on the FOREARM (not lower extremity). DFU is body-area specific.

patient.name: Marlene Hodge

radiology.finding: Positive for underlying osteomyelitis of the radius
Positive for underlying osteomyelitis of the radius

patient.clinical_notes: Patient is a 67-year-old female with long-standing Type 1 diabetes managed on insulin pump. She presents with a chronic non-healing wound on the dorsal aspect of the right forearm, present for approximately 8 weeks. The wound was initially sustained as a minor abrasion from a fall in her garden. Despite standard wound care including debridements, moist dressings, and offloading via sling support, the wound has not improved. MRI 01/05/2026 confirmed underlying osteomyelitis of the radius.

prior_osteomyelitis_same_location.evidence: MRI 01/05/2026 positive for osteomyelitis of the radius

confirming_radiology_pathology_lab.evidence: MRI 01/05/2026 confirms osteomyelitis; Xray 02/15/2026 confirms osteomyelitis

antibiotics_or_surgery.evidence: Two debridements (02/02/2026 and 03/05/2026); SWC ongoing; IV Vancomycin

cases.teaching_moment: Classic DFU trap. Patient has diabetes, a chronic wound, documented standard wound care, debridements, and positive imaging for osteomyelitis. BUT — the wound is on the right forearm. The DFU indication under CMS covers Diabetic Foot Ulcers specifically, defined as Wounds of the Lower Extremity (leg, ankle, foot, toes). The arm, hand, or any upper extremity wound is NOT eligible under DFU regardless of how diabetic the patient is. So how do we screen this patient? Under Chronic Refractory Osteomyelitis (CROM) — which IS anatomy-agnostic and DOES apply here, since the patient has confirmed osteomyelitis, refractory to current management. CROM is the right call. Lesson: always validate body location against the indication's anatomic scope before committing.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L4 — Documentation Gap. Patient clinically qualifies for ORN, but the cGy amount is not in the chart. Must kick back for documentation before submitting.

S/P Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the lung

radiology.finding: Soft tissue radiation changes left chest wall, no recurrent malignancy

patient.clinical_notes: Patient with history of left lung squamous cell carcinoma, treated with chemoradiation in 2023 followed by surgical excision of residual chest wall lesion in November 2024. Patient now presents 18 months later with delayed wound dehiscence and soft tissue breakdown of the left chest wall consistent with soft tissue radionecrosis. Provider notes patient received radiotherapy 'in 2023' — specific cGy amount and end date not documented in current chart. Patient reports completing 'six weeks of daily radiation' but cannot provide records.
patient.radiotherapy: Radiotherapy in 2023 — specific cGy and end date NOT documented in current chart

cases.teaching_moment: This patient is clinically eligible for HBOT under Soft Tissue Radionecrosis — the diagnosis is documented, the signs and symptoms are documented, and the imaging is consistent. BUT the chart is missing two required STRN criteria: documented amount of radiation (minimum 4,000 cGy) and documented end date of treatment. Patient self-reports 'six weeks of daily radiation' which is suggestive but not adequate. Without the specific cGy total and end date, the screening fails CMS documentation requirements. Next step: contact the patient's radiation oncology provider to obtain treatment records before submitting the HBOT screening. Once those records arrive and confirm ≥4,000 cGy and an end date, re-screen and proceed. This is NOT a denial — it's a 'not yet, get the documentation first.'

cases.difficulty_explanation: L4 — Documentation Gap. CROM clinical case missing the antibiotic course documentation.

patient.name: Patricia Llewellyn

radiology.finding: Positive for osteomyelitis, right tibial shaft
Positive for persistent osteomyelitis, right tibial shaft

patient.clinical_notes: Patient is a 53-year-old female with history of open tibial fracture in August 2024 (motor vehicle accident), treated with ORIF. Developed deep infection postoperatively. Recent imaging confirms chronic osteomyelitis of the right tibia. Patient underwent surgical bone debridement on 01/10/2026 with continued symptoms. Repeat MRI 03/05/2026 shows persistent osteomyelitis despite surgical intervention. Outside hospital records of post-surgical antibiotic management not available; patient reports 'a few rounds of IV antibiotics' but cannot recall specifics.

cases.teaching_moment: This patient is clinically a CROM candidate — confirmed osteomyelitis in the same location across two MRIs three months apart, with documented surgical debridement that did not resolve the infection. BUT CMS coverage for CROM requires documented antibiotics AND/OR surgery — and while the surgery is documented, the antibiotic management is only patient-reported ('a few rounds of IV antibiotics'). Best practice is to obtain the outside hospital records documenting the specific antibiotic regimens (drug, duration, route) before submitting. Even though 'and/or' technically means surgery alone could suffice, a typical CROM presentation includes ~6 weeks of antibiotic therapy, and auditors will look for it. Recommendation: request records from the treating hospital, document the antibiotic course, then re-screen.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L5 — Curveball. Diabetic patient with osteomyelitis of the elbow. DFU is the obvious wrong answer (lower extremity only). Correct answer is CROM.

patient.name: Reginald Cobb

radiology.finding: Positive for osteomyelitis, distal humerus
Persistent osteomyelitis, distal humerus, despite surgical and antibiotic therapy

patient.clinical_notes: 58-year-old male with Type 2 Diabetes presenting with persistent right elbow osteomyelitis following open reduction of a traumatic elbow injury sustained in October 2025. Despite surgical debridement on 01/20/2026 and six weeks of IV Vancomycin, MRI on 03/01/2026 demonstrates persistent osteomyelitis of the distal humerus. Patient reports continued pain, swelling, and restricted range of motion at the elbow.

prior_osteomyelitis_same_location.evidence: MRI 12/05/2025 positive for osteomyelitis of distal humerus

antibiotics_or_surgery.evidence: Six weeks IV Vancomycin + surgical debridement 01/20/2026

cases.teaching_moment: Quiz Q8 made real. Diabetic patient with osteomyelitis — DFU instinct fires hard. But the osteomyelitis is in the ELBOW (distal humerus, upper extremity). The DFU indication under CMS is strictly defined: diabetic wounds of the LOWER extremity only (leg, ankle, foot, toes). Any upper extremity site — arm, elbow, hand, shoulder — is excluded from DFU regardless of how diabetic the patient is. The correct indication is Chronic Refractory Osteomyelitis (CROM), which has no anatomic restriction. Patient meets all three CROM criteria: prior osteomyelitis confirmed (12/05/2025), persistent on repeat imaging (03/01/2026), and documented antibiotic + surgical management that has failed. CROM is the call. Lesson: 'diabetic + osteomyelitis' is not automatically DFU. Always check body location against indication scope first.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L5 — Curveball. Radionecrosis patient at 2 months post-radiation (typically too early — guidance is 4+ months). Tests whether trainee knows the timing standard.

patient.name: Constance Whittaker
dx: Soft Tissue Radionecrosis, left breast/chest wall
S/P Invasive Ductal Carcinoma, left breast

radiology.finding: Soft tissue inflammation and small areas of necrosis consistent with early radiation injury

patient.clinical_notes: 60-year-old female S/P lumpectomy for invasive ductal carcinoma in August 2025, followed by adjuvant radiation. Patient completed radiotherapy on 01/15/2026 (4500 cGy total, left breast/chest wall). Now presenting two months post-treatment with early signs of radiation skin changes and soft tissue breakdown. Provider referring for HBOT evaluation. Patient reports mild discomfort and skin tightness.
patient.radiotherapy: 4500 cGy to left breast/chest wall concluded on 01/15/2026

cases.teaching_moment: Every STRN criterion appears met on the chart — radiation amount, location, end date, signs/symptoms. BUT the timing is wrong. Radiation concluded on 01/15/2026 and review date is 03/15/2026 — only TWO months post-treatment. Per Palmetto GBA and broader UHMS guidance, radionecrosis treatment is 'typically at least 4 months post-radiation.' This patient is presenting too early. Early post-radiation skin changes are common and often resolve with standard wound care alone. HBOT is reserved for established radionecrosis that has had time to declare itself and fail conservative management. The right call here is NOT to screen the patient as eligible STRN at this time. Recommendation: continue standard wound care, document the trajectory, re-evaluate at the 4-month mark and beyond if symptoms persist. Lesson: documentation completeness is necessary but not sufficient — timing standards matter too.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L1 — clean Compromised Flap case (tibia fx + flap rotation). All criteria documented w/ clear evidence.

patient.name: Walter Greene
dx: Compromised fasciocutaneous flap, right lower leg

surgeries.procedure: Fasciocutaneous flap rotation w/ donor site STSG

radiology.finding: Open midshaft fracture w/ ORIF hardware placement

radiology.study: Doppler arterial study right lower leg
radiology.finding: Diminished perfusion at flap distal third

patient.clinical_notes: 54-year-old male S/P open right tibia fracture sustained in workplace accident 11/15/2025, requiring ORIF. Wound broke down post-operatively w/ plate over tibia becoming exposed. Fasciocutaneous flap rotated to cover exposed plate and bone 02/03/2026, w/ donor site skin grafted behind it. At post-op day 7, distal third of flap demonstrates dusky/cyanotic appearance w/ impending necrosis. Failing flap protocol initiated. The compromised distal portion of the flap is the critical tissue covering the exposed orthopedic hardware — flap failure would expose the plate and create a much larger reconstruction problem.

graft_compromised.evidence: Distal third of flap dusky/cyanotic w/ impending necrosis

tissue_hypoxia_demonstrated.evidence: TCOM PO2 22 mmHg at flap distal edge 02/10/2026

cases.teaching_moment: Textbook Compromised Flap presentation. Clear surgical date for flap creation (02/03/2026), unambiguous documentation of flap compromise (distal third dusky and cyanotic w/ impending necrosis), and tissue hypoxia objectively measured by TCOM at the flap edge (22 mmHg). The clinical stakes are explicit — the distal flap is covering exposed orthopedic hardware over a tibia fracture. If the flap dies, the hardware re-exposes and the patient is looking at amputation-level reconstruction or worse. This is what a clean Compromised Flap referral looks like: surgical date, evidence of compromise, ideally objective tissue hypoxia documentation, and clear clinical stakes that justify the intervention.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L1 — clean Compromised Flap, transmetatarsal amputation w/ non-healing flap post-bypass.

patient.name: Earl Pemberton

surgeries.procedure: Distal fem-tib bypass, right lower extremity

radiology.finding: Bypass graft patent; pulsatile flow at medial malleolus
Post-surgical changes consistent with transmetatarsal amputation; no acute osseous abnormality

patient.clinical_notes: 70-year-old male w/ history of severe peripheral vascular disease, S/P distal fem-tib bypass 01/31/2026 followed by right transmetatarsal amputation 02/07/2026. Three months post-operatively, the distal flap demonstrates non-healing and cyanosis. BKA (below-knee amputation) has been considered as a salvage option. HBOT consultation placed to attempt flap salvage by promoting survival without need for additional surgical revision.

graft_compromised.evidence: Non-healing cyanotic flap, five days post-op

tissue_hypoxia_demonstrated.evidence: TCOM PO2 29 mmHg right foot dorsum 02/05/2026

cases.teaching_moment: For HBOT purposes the term compromised flap does not exclusively refer to a free flap or fasciocutaneous rotational flap—it includes any surgically created flap or graft. In this case, the patient underwent a transmetatarsal amputation with flap creation, and the surgical site has subsequently failed to heal despite a patent bypass graft. The clinical significance is substantial, as the alternative treatment option may be a below-knee amputation (BKA). HBOT is being utilized as a limb-salvage intervention to support flap viability and promote healing while avoiding additional surgical revision. The documentation supports coverage criteria with a clearly identified surgical date (02/07/2026), evidence of flap compromise (cyanotic appearance), and objective confirmation of tissue hypoxia demonstrated by a TCOM PO2 of 29 mmHg. This represents a well-supported compromised flap case.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L2 — 58yo brittle Type 1 diabetic w/ foot wound + history of failed STSG. Two indications could plausibly fit (DFU vs Compromised Graft). Detective work required to pick the right pathway.

patient.name: Lorraine Pickett
dx: Chronic non-healing wound left lateral foot

surgeries.procedure: Split-thickness skin graft, left lateral foot

radiology.finding: Positive for osteomyelitis of the 5th metatarsal head

patient.clinical_notes: 58-year-old female w/ longstanding Type 1 brittle diabetes, two ER visits in the past 18 months for DKA and one for severe hypoglycemia. CGM data demonstrates wide glucose variability despite basal/bolus insulin regimen. Patient presents w/ chronic non-healing wound left lateral foot, present approximately 7 months. Underwent femoral-AT bypass 04/15/2025 w/ subsequent improvement in toe pressures. Attempted STSG 11/04/2025 which failed within 2 weeks. Wound demonstrates pale granulation tissue; TCOM PO2 28 mmHg on room air is subnormal. X-ray 02/10/2026 positive for osteomyelitis of 5th metatarsal head — newly documented. Started on IV Vancomycin 02/12/2026 for osteomyelitis. Standard wound care continuing.

wagner_3_or_higher.evidence: X-ray 02/10/2026 positive for osteomyelitis 5th metatarsal head

30_days_swc.evidence: Wound 7 months duration, multiple debridements 12/18/2025 + 02/06/2026, ongoing SWC documented

no_measurable_healing.evidence: Wound 14.4 cm² 11/05/25 to 14.4 cm² 02/15/26 — no measurable healing over 3+ months

documented_vascular_assessment.evidence: TCOM PO2 28 mmHg left foot; toe pressures improved post-bypass

documented_infection_treatment.evidence: IV Vancomycin started 02/12/2026 + surgical debridements 12/18/2025 and 02/06/2026

cases.teaching_moment: Two indications compete here, and the smart pick depends on what just changed in the chart. Compromised Graft pathway is tempting — patient has a failed STSG (11/04/2025), documented tissue hypoxia (TCOM 28 mmHg), and the language 'failed graft' in the Dx. BUT the STSG was attempted 4 months ago — that surgical wound has long since either succeeded or failed, and what we're now treating is the persistent UNDERLYING wound that the STSG was attempting to close. The current driver of the wound is diabetic vascular disease + new osteomyelitis (02/10/2026 X-ray) of the 5th metatarsal head. That kicks the case into DFU territory: Type 1 diabetic, lower extremity wound, Wagner Grade III (positive radiology for osteomyelitis), 7 months of documented SWC w/ no measurable healing, all supporting elements present. HbA1c 8.4 is poorly controlled BUT 'glucose control' criterion requires documented monitoring, not necessarily WELL-controlled values — the brittle diabetic status is itself documented evidence of glucose management complexity. Lesson: when multiple indications COULD fit, ask which one captures the CURRENT clinical driver of the wound, not the historical context. The STSG failure is history. The osteomyelitis is now.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L4 — Documentation Gap variant of the brittle IDDM scenario: the chart is missing the radiology to confirm Wagner Grade III.

patient.name: Vivian Crowder
dx: Chronic non-healing wound right plantar foot

surgeries.date: Date NOT documented in current chart

surgeries.procedure: Split-thickness skin graft, right plantar foot

patient.clinical_notes: 58-year-old brittle Type 1 diabetic female on insulin pump. Chronic non-healing wound right plantar foot, approximately 5 months duration. Failed STSG attempt 10/22/2025. Outside facility records indicate prior femoral-popliteal bypass but specific date and pre/post pressure values not transferred to current chart. Wound has not measurably progressed despite SWC and one sharp debridement. No imaging of the affected foot has been performed at this facility. Clinical exam suggests deep wound but no documented osteomyelitis screening. Provider considering HBOT referral but screening team has questions about documentation completeness.

cases.teaching_moment: Clinically this patient is very likely eligible for HBOT — brittle Type 1 diabetic, chronic non-healing wound 5+ months, failed graft history, multiple SWC elements all documented. BUT the chart is missing the imaging required to establish Wagner Grade III. For the DFU pathway, you need positive radiology results (osteomyelitis, abscess) OR positive deep wound culture showing moderate-to-heavy growth. Neither is in the chart. The clinical exam 'suggests deep wound' but no X-ray, MRI, or culture has been performed. For the Compromised Graft pathway, the STSG date (10/22/2025) IS documented but the wound is now 4 months old — it's no longer functionally a graft failure, it's a chronic diabetic wound. Right call: kick back for imaging. Order X-ray of affected foot (and MRI if X-ray inconclusive) to assess for osteomyelitis. If positive, DFU pathway opens cleanly. If negative, consider deep wound culture or reconsider whether patient truly qualifies. Don't ship the screening without the imaging — auditor will catch it.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L2 — Chart documents nec fasc protocol treatment in the acute phase, but current screening is for chronic phase DFU. Trainee must recognize that 'nec fasc protocol' in chart history is treatment context, not current indication.

patient.name: Eleanor Mathis
dx: S/P necrotizing wound w/ tendon exposure
Chronic non-healing diabetic foot ulcer left forefoot

labs.value: 30 mmHg room air; 1,162 mmHg under HBOT

radiology.finding: Soft tissue changes consistent with chronic infection; no acute osseous abnormality

patient.clinical_notes: 69-year-old brittle Type 2 diabetic female who developed pressure necrosis of the left forefoot resulting in a complicated necrotizing wound with tendon exposure. Patient required emergent I&D and debridement on 01/05/2026. Initial presentation included signs concerning for necrotizing infection — patient was started on the necrotizing fasciitis protocol for 72 hours per UHMS guidelines. Despite normal toe pressures, transcutaneous oxygen tension was 30 mmHg on room air, increasing to 1,162 mmHg at 2.0 ATA hyperbaric oxygen. After 72 hours of nec fasc protocol with clinical stabilization, patient was converted to the problem wound (DFU) protocol per UHMS recognition. Wound has stabilized but is not progressing — multiple debridements (02/02/2026 and 02/23/2026) and ongoing IV Vancomycin for the documented deep wound infection (Staph aureus + Strep). Deep wound culture from 01/05/2026 confirms moderate-to-heavy growth establishing Wagner Grade III status. Patient now in chronic DFU phase, screening for ongoing HBOT continuation under problem wound indication.

wagner_3_or_higher.evidence: Deep wound culture and I&D on 01/05/2026. Culture positive for moderate growth Staph aureus and Strep.

30_days_swc.evidence: I&D 01/05/2026 + debridements 02/02/2026 and 02/23/2026, ongoing SWC documented (55+ days)

no_measurable_healing.evidence: Wound 12.0 cm² on 01/05/26 to 11.5 cm² on 02/23/26 — minimal healing over 7+ weeks

documented_vascular_assessment.evidence: Normal toe pressures 01/20/2026; TCOM PO2 30 mmHg room air, 1,162 mmHg under HBOT

cases.teaching_moment: The chart documents necrotizing fasciitis protocol treatment in the acute phase, but the SCREENING question is what indication applies for ongoing HBOT NOW. The nec fasc protocol phase ended after 72 hours — patient was converted to the problem wound (DFU) protocol per UHMS guidelines once acute symptoms stabilized. Current screening is happening 8 weeks into the chronic phase. The indication question = DFU. All DFU criteria are documented: Type 2 diabetes, Wagner Grade III established by I&D and positive deep wound culture (Staph aureus + Strep moderate growth — note this is the culture pathway to Wagner III, not the radiology pathway), 30+ days of documented SWC w/ multiple debridements, no measurable healing, glucose control documented, vascular (normal toe pressures), nutrition, dressings, and infection treatment (Vancomycin + debridements). Lesson: treatment history ≠ current screening indication. The nec fasc protocol was the acute-phase treatment; DFU is the chronic-phase screening.'

cases.difficulty_explanation: L1 — clean STRN case (sarcoma adjuvant radiation → soft tissue radiation necrosis of right medial knee). All four STRN criteria clearly documented w/ chart-visible evidence. Dates place STRN well past the 4-month UHMS threshold (8 months post-radiation at review).

patient.name: Calvin Hodges
dx: S/P malignant fibrohistiocytoma right medial knee
S/P wide excision + adjuvant radiation therapy
Soft tissue radiation necrosis (STRN), right medial knee

surgeries.procedure: Wide excision of malignant fibrohistiocytoma, right medial knee

radiology.finding: Soft tissue necrosis w/ deep cavitation, no evidence of recurrent malignancy or osteomyelitis

patient.clinical_notes: 64-year-old male S/P wide excision of malignant fibrohistiocytoma of the right medial knee on 03/10/2025, followed by adjuvant external beam radiation therapy. Radiation completed 05/15/2025 for a total dose of 6000 cGy delivered per sarcoma protocol. Patient did well through the immediate post-radiation period. Approximately six months following completion of radiation, patient developed complete wound dehiscence of the surgical site with progressive soft tissue radiation necrosis. Initial dehiscence noted 11/2025 w/ open cavity and purulent drainage. Wound now estimated Stage III/IV ulceration, measuring 9 x 6.5 cm. Currently on oral antibiotics for the documented wound infection. MRI 12/15/2025 confirms soft tissue necrosis w/ deep cavitation, no recurrent malignancy or underlying osteomyelitis. Now 8 months post-radiation, presenting for HBOT screening to address established soft tissue radionecrosis.

radiation_amount.evidence: 6000 cGy total radiation dose (exceeds 4000 cGy minimum)

anatomical_location.evidence: Right medial knee — radiation field documented

end_date_of_tx.evidence: Radiation completed 05/15/2025 (8 months prior to review)

signs_symptoms_of_injury.evidence: Wound dehiscence, soft tissue radiation necrosis, open cavity w/ purulent drainage, Stage III/IV ulceration

cases.teaching_moment: Textbook STRN screening. All four STRN criteria documented w/ clear chart evidence: (1) Radiation amount — 6000 cGy total dose, well above the 4000 cGy minimum threshold and consistent with sarcoma adjuvant protocol. (2) Anatomical location — right medial knee, both the surgical site and the radiation field. (3) End date of treatment — radiation completed 05/15/2025, placing the review (01/15/2026) at 8 months post-radiation, well past the 4-month UHMS threshold for STRN to declare itself and fail conservative management. (4) Signs and symptoms — wound dehiscence, soft tissue radiation necrosis, open cavity with purulent drainage, Stage III/IV ulceration. This is what a clean STRN referral looks like: dose documented, location documented, timing well past the 4-month threshold, and the wound has declared itself with unambiguous clinical signs with appropriate adjunctive therapies.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L1 — clean Crush Injury case (industrial hand crush w/ palmar skin avulsion + thumb fractures). The threatening loss of function is documented unambiguously by the surgical assessment: distal portion of palmar flap not expected to survive at time of surgery. Acute presentation, time-critical screening.

patient.name: Marcus Wheeler
dx: Avulsion of palmar skin, right hand
Comminuted fractures, right thumb (proximal and distal phalanx)

surgeries.procedure: Surgical debridement, primary closure of avulsed palmar skin, pin fixation of right thumb fractures

radiology.finding: Comminuted fractures of right thumb proximal and distal phalanx; soft tissue swelling consistent with crush injury

patient.wound_dressing: Non-adherent moist gauze w/ outer wrap, hand splinted
patient.clinical_notes: 38-year-old male sustained a crush injury to his right hand when caught between a conveyor belt and roller at his workplace on 02/18/2026. Presented to ED with significant avulsion of the palmar skin, comminuted fractures of the right thumb, and obvious crush mechanism. Taken emergently to OR for surgical debridement, primary closure of the avulsed palmar skin, and pin fixation of the thumb fractures. At time of surgery, the distal portion of the palmar flap was assessed as NOT expected to survive — distal flap noted as non-viable based on examination — a vertical line of demarcation was marked through the mid-palm denoting the area of compromised tissue. Post-operative plan includes initiation of hyperbaric oxygen therapy per crush injury protocol to maximize tissue salvage of the compromised flap. Screening review for HBOT scheduled morning following surgery (within 24 hours of injury) — acute presentation, time-critical intervention.

threatening_loss_function_limb_life.evidence: Avulsion of palmar skin w/ distal flap not expected to survive (per surgical assessment 02/18/2026)

cases.teaching_moment: Textbook Crush Injury screening. The CMS criterion is broad — documentation of threatening loss of function, limb, or life — and the chart needs to demonstrate at least one of those three. This case documents BOTH function loss AND limb threat: avulsion of palmar skin (significant function impairment of the hand), and distal portion of palmar flap not expected to survive based on the surgeon's direct examination at time of surgery. The marking of a vertical line of demarcation through mid-palm at surgery is itself audit-defensible documentation — the operating surgeon, in real time, identified the at-risk tissue and documented it. HBOT is being initiated per crush injury protocol within 24 hours of injury, which is the acute-phase timing when the indication is most effective. Note: the comminuted thumb fractures and the K-wire fixation, while real injuries in this chart, are not the primary threatening-loss-of-function documentation — fractures alone don't establish the criterion. The audit-defensible citations are the avulsion + flap viability assessment. Trainees who cite the thumb fractures as their evidence have identified injuries but not the criterion-relevant evidence. Clean Crush Injury referral: acute mechanism documented, immediate surgical intervention, threatening loss of function unambiguously assessed by the surgeon, acute-phase HBOT initiation within hours of injury.

patient.clinical_notes: 4-year-old male slipped and fell into a riding lawnmower sustaining a mid-calf amputation of the right lower extremity. Patient was transported to ED with the severed limb preserved on ice. Time from injury to vascular reattachment was approximately 10 hours. Patient taken emergently to OR for microvascular replantation with anastomosis of the posterior tibial artery, posterior tibial vein, and tibial nerve; external fixation placed for skeletal stability. Surgery was technically successful — macrovascular continuity restored, weak but detectable distal arterial signal documented on post-op Doppler. However, given the approximately 10-hour ischemia time, the replanted limb is at high risk for reperfusion injury, microvascular thrombosis, and tissue-level acute ischemia despite the successful macrovascular repair. Elevated lactate (3.4) and CK (4,200) consistent with ischemic muscle injury. HBOT initiated per acute traumatic peripheral ischemia protocol — 90 minutes at 2.4 ATA every 8 hours for first 24 hours, transitioning to every 12 hours for subsequent treatments. Screening review for HBOT continuation on post-op day 1 — acute-phase intervention, time-critical for limb salvage.

cases.teaching_moment: Textbook Acute Traumatic Peripheral Ischemia screening. Two clinical phases to understand: the macrovascular disruption (severed limb) was resolved surgically by replantation with anastomosis of the posterior tibial artery and vein. That part is done. BUT the limb spent approximately 10 hours without blood flow before reperfusion, which puts the tissue at acute risk despite the successful surgical repair — reperfusion injury, microvascular thrombosis, and tissue-level ischemia are all active concerns. HBOT addresses the tissue-level acute ischemia that surgery alone cannot fix. Criterion #1 (threatening loss of function/limb/life): unambiguous — the limb was severed and replanted, and survival of the limb is the active clinical question. Criterion #2 (acute onset of ischemia of extremity): the 10-hour ischemia time is the audit-defensible citation — the chart documents the duration explicitly, and the elevated lactate (3.4 mmol/L) and CK (4,200 U/L) provide objective biochemical evidence of ischemic muscle injury. HBOT initiated within 24 hours of injury per Acute Traumatic Peripheral Ischemia protocol. This is what a clean acute-trauma referral looks like: dramatic mechanism documented, surgical intervention completed, the residual ischemic threat documented with specific timeframe and lab evidence, and HBOT initiated in the acute window when the indication is most effective.

patient.clinical_notes: 57-year-old male presenting w/ rapidly progressive abdominal wall necrosis. Past medical history significant for Type 2 diabetes mellitus, otherwise unremarkable. Approximately two weeks prior to admission, patient underwent oral surgery (third molar extractions w/ management of a dental abscess) — believed to be the precipitating event. Patient developed increasing pain and erythema of the abdominal wall over several days, progressing to obvious necrotic changes prompting ED presentation. On admission, WBC 22,400, lactate 3.1, CRP 28.4, CT showing subcutaneous gas + fat stranding consistent with necrotizing soft tissue infection. Wide-spectrum antibiotics (Pip-Tazo + Vancomycin + Clindamycin) initiated immediately. Radical debridement performed 02/20/2026 for rapidly progressive necrosis — large abdominal wall defect created (32 x 18 cm). Intraoperative cultures grew polymicrobial flora (Streptococcus pyogenes + anaerobes) consistent with Type II necrotizing fasciitis. Patient was discharged on hospital day 5 and started HBOT the following day per nec fasc adjunct protocol. On day 2 of HBOT, VAC placed at 175 mmHg continuous w/ Acticoat Burn underlay (first 4 dressing changes). Screening review for HBOT continuation on 02/26/2026 — acute phase, time-critical adjunct to surgical management.

cases.teaching_moment: Diabetes is present in this chart but it is not the driver of this screening. Multiple disqualifiers from the DFU pathway are visible if the trainee reads the chart: (1) Wound location is abdominal wall, not lower extremity — DFU requires a foot or lower extremity wound. (2) Onset was rapidly progressive over days, not chronic non-healing over 30+ days — DFU requires documented standard wound care failure. (3) Etiology is post-surgical infection (dental abscess as the precipitating source) seeding hematogenous spread to abdominal wall, not diabetic vascular or neuropathic. (4) Treatment is radical debridement + wide-spectrum antibiotics + immediate adjunct HBOT — the acute nec fasc protocol, not chronic wound care escalation. The audit-defensible screening here is NEC_FASC: documented progressive necrotizing infection (CT findings + intraoperative polymicrobial cultures confirm Type II necrotizing fasciitis), HBOT used as adjunct to aggressive surgical debridement + antibiotic therapy (chart explicitly documents this protocol). Diabetes is a comorbidity that increased the patient's risk for nec fasc development, but is not the screening indication. Lesson: when a chart contains diabetes plus a severe wound, ask what KIND of wound — chronic ulcer with documented SWC failure (DFU) vs rapidly progressive necrotizing infection (NEC_FASC). The temporal pattern, anatomical location, and treatment protocol are all visible discriminators.

cases.teaching_moment: The criterion requires documentation of acute ischemia caused by an arterial mechanism, and this chart clearly supports that requirement. The provider explicitly documents “acute arterial insufficiency, left foot,” with postoperative vascular compromise caused by an embolus occurring two days after elective surgery, establishing an acute arterial event. Objective evidence is also present, with arterial Doppler findings showing reduced arterial flow and an ABI decline to 0.6 from baseline. The threatened-limb component is clearly documented through references to threatened toes, threatened forefoot, and possible below-knee amputation (BKA). The HBOT consult further supports coverage by documenting threatened loss of adjoining toes, possible forefoot amputation, and possible BKA. Key takeaway: audit-defensible proof of arterial compromise does not require exact criterion wording—an explicit arterial diagnosis, acute onset, objective vascular findings, and documented threat to limb viability are sufficient to support coverage.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L2 — Chart presents as acute stroke workup (GCS 9, dysarthria, motor weakness, CT head obtained) with NSTEMI overlay (troponin trajectory 198 → 587 → 741 ng/L, T-wave inversions). The acute carbon monoxide exposure is documented in the chart but buried under stroke-mimic + cardiac noise. Trainees fixated on the neuro/cardiac presentation will punt to DOES_NOT_QUALIFY thinking 'this is an ICU patient, not an HBOT screening.' The chart-reading lesson: ACUTE_CO criterion is satisfied by documented exposure source (charcoal heater) + diagnostic confirmation (COHb 32.8%) regardless of the multi-system clinical noise — and the multi-system involvement (neuro + cardiac) is exactly the indication profile HBOT is recommended for in CO poisoning. Source: NIH PMC12247657 — Al Lawati et al., 82F charcoal heater exposure, stroke-mimic presentation, successful HBOT.

patient.clinical_notes: 82-year-old female with past medical history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and ischemic heart disease who presented to the emergency department on 01/14/2026 with progressively worsening mental status, flu-like symptoms (nausea, vomiting, headache), and slurred speech that developed approximately 6 hours prior to arrival. Patient lives in Paintsville, KY and was found by her son near-unconscious approximately 2-3 meters from a charcoal-burning heater that she had been using for warmth during a winter cold snap. On arrival, GCS 9/15 (E2V2M5), dysarthria, motor weakness 2/5 in all extremities with localization to painful stimuli. Vital signs hemodynamically stable on room air (HR 92, BP 110/68, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temp 38.2°C). Initial workup obtained to evaluate for cerebrovascular event given altered mental status and focal neurologic findings. CT head non-contrast ruled out acute intracranial process. Venous blood gas analysis returned COHb 32.8%, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, establishing diagnosis of acute carbon monoxide intoxication. Chest X-ray showed diffuse reticular shadowing consistent with pulmonary edema. Serial troponin demonstrated significant elevation (peak 741 ng/L) with non-specific T-wave inversions on ECG, consistent with type II myocardial infarction secondary to cellular hypoxia from CO binding. Patient placed on high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask immediately on diagnosis. After 2 hours of normobaric oxygen therapy, COHb dropped to 9.4% but clinical improvement was minimal — patient remained obtunded with persistent neurologic deficits. Toxicology consulted; recommendation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy given persistent neurologic manifestations + elevated troponin + initial COHb >25%. HBOT screening review on 01/14/2026.

acute_co_exposure.evidence: Patient found near-unconscious with progressively worsening mental status, flu-like symptoms (nausea, vomiting, headache), and slurred speech within 2-3 meters from active charcoal-burning heater used for indoor heating; venous blood gas on admission confirmed COHb 32.8% (severely elevated, threshold for HBOT indication is ≥25%); lactate 3.1 mmol/L supporting cellular hypoxia; minimal clinical improvement after 2 hours of normobaric oxygen despite COHb level drop

cases.teaching_moment: The trap on this chart is symptom noise overwhelming indication recognition. Trainee scans, sees acute neurologic + cardiac + pulmonary findings in an elderly comorbid patient, and concludes 'this is an ICU multi-system illness, not an HBOT screening' → punts to DOES_NOT_QUALIFY. That is the wrong call. The chart documents acute carbon monoxide intoxication explicitly: known exposure source (charcoal-burning heater used indoors for warmth, patient found near-unconscious 2-3 meters from the source) + objective diagnostic confirmation (COHb 32.8% on admission venous blood gas, well above the 25% threshold that triggers HBOT consideration per UHMS guidelines) + supporting evidence (elevated lactate 3.1 mmol/L from cellular hypoxia, minimal clinical improvement despite 2 hours of normobaric oxygen, persistent neurologic deficits, type II MI from CO-induced cellular hypoxia). The multi-system involvement — altered mental status, flu-like symptoms (nausea, vomiting, headache), slurred speech, persistent neurologic deficits, elevated troponin — is not a reason to exclude HBOT; it is exactly the clinical profile for which HBOT is recommended in CO poisoning (severe poisoning with cardiac or neurologic symptoms). The criterion 'Documented acute carbon monoxide exposure' is satisfied unambiguously by the charcoal heater exposure history plus the COHb level. The audit-defensible documentation chain is: exposure source + COHb level + clinical manifestations. Lesson: ACUTE_CO is an HBOT indication. Recognize it under symptom noise. Do not punt acute toxicology cases because they don't look like outpatient wound care — the screening question is whether the chart documents acute CO exposure, and this one does, cold.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L2 — Patient presents to ED with shoulder pain + fatigue + skin findings 18 hours after returning home from a Florida Keys vacation. The chart documents two dives on the trip's final day with a same-day return flight approximately 4 hours after the last surface — the textbook 'flying after diving' violation (DAN recommends minimum 12-24 hour surface interval before flight). Trainees fixated on the joint pain workup or post-travel viral framing will miss the timing-gap detective work. Symptoms are also classic Type I DCS (musculoskeletal + cutis marmorata) but vague enough that the indication recognition depends entirely on catching the dive + flight history in the chart. Over-cautious trainees may demand dive computer logs, depth profiles, or surface interval calculations before screening — kicking to NEED_MORE_INFO when the criterion is already satisfied by the documented dive + same-day flight sequence. Sources: NIH PMC11537778 (Remmel et al. — Type I DCS clinical presentation, cutis marmorata, musculoskeletal pain pattern) + real-world SHS partner pattern (vacation diver → same-day flight → DCS presentation post-arrival).

patient.clinical_notes: 46-year-old male, otherwise healthy, presents to the emergency department on 03/16/2026 with right shoulder pain, fatigue, and a 'mottled red rash' on the right anterior chest that began approximately 18 hours prior to arrival. Patient returned home to East Tennessee on the evening of 03/15/2026 from a five-day recreational scuba diving vacation in Key Largo, Florida. Per patient's account, he completed two boat dives on the morning of 03/15/2026 (last day of trip): first dive to approximately 70 feet for 35 minutes, second dive to approximately 55 feet for 40 minutes, with a 90-minute surface interval between dives. Patient and dive buddy left the dive boat around 12:00 PM and flew home on a commercial flight that departed Miami at approximately 4:00 PM the same day — total surface interval before flight was approximately 4 hours. Patient reports feeling 'achy and tired' during the flight which he initially attributed to travel fatigue. Symptoms worsened overnight after arrival home with development of right shoulder pain (rated 6/10), inability to fully abduct the arm, and a 'lacy red rash' across the right anterior chest. Wife encouraged ED visit after patient took ibuprofen at home without improvement. Patient denies neurologic symptoms, no headache, no visual changes, no paresthesia, no weakness, no chest pain, no shortness of breath. Vital signs stable on arrival (HR 84, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, afebrile). Physical exam confirms cutis marmorata of right anterior chest and reduced active range of motion of the right shoulder secondary to pain. No focal neuro deficits. Workup obtained to evaluate for thromboembolic event, musculoskeletal injury, and viral illness was unrevealing — labs unremarkable, D-dimer negative, Doppler negative, X-ray showing only baseline degenerative changes. Detailed history-taking on the second pass identified the recent dive trip + same-day return flight as the precipitating decompression event. Patient placed on high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather. Diagnosis of Type I decompression sickness made on clinical grounds. HBOT screening review on 03/16/2026 for recompression therapy.

decompression_event.evidence: Two recreational dives on 03/15/2026 (70 feet x 35 min + 55 feet x 40 min) followed by commercial flight from Miami the same day approximately 4 hours after last surface — well below the DAN-recommended 12-24 hour minimum surface interval before flight. Symptom onset within 18 hours of the decompression event, with clinical presentation consistent with Type I DCS (musculoskeletal pain + cutis marmorata).

cases.teaching_moment: The trap on this chart is the symptom story burying the timing story. Trainees who scan the chief complaint (shoulder pain + rash + fatigue) without catching the dive + same-day flight history will work the case as a post-travel musculoskeletal-or-viral problem and miss the indication entirely. The criterion is 'Documented decompression event (diving, altitude, etc.)' — the chart documents BOTH triggers in sequence: two recreational dives on 03/15/2026 (70 feet and 55 feet) followed by a commercial flight approximately 4 hours after the last surface. The DAN guideline minimum surface interval before flight is 12-24 hours; this patient flew at 4 hours. That sequence IS the decompression event. The clinical presentation (musculoskeletal pain + cutis marmorata + constitutional symptoms onset within 24 hours) is the textbook Type I DCS pattern, but the indication-defining documentation is the dive + flight history — not the symptoms or the labs. Note that DCS diagnosis is clinical: unremarkable labs and imaging do NOT exclude the diagnosis. Lesson: when a patient presents with vague musculoskeletal + constitutional symptoms within hours-to-days of air travel or diving, the dive history is the indication-defining documentation. The screening criterion is satisfied by a documented decompression event, and 'dove this morning then flew this afternoon' is documented decompression event by definition. Do not demand dive computer logs or depth profile calculations before screening — those refine clinical understanding but the criterion is already met.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L2 — Chart documents an intra-operative venous gas embolism event during hysteroscopic fibroid resection (millwheel murmur, sudden EtCO2 drop, 2D ECHO confirming air bubbles in right atrium, anesthesia crisis successfully managed with Durant's maneuver + 100% O2 + supportive care). Patient hemodynamically stabilized intra-op BUT emerged from anesthesia with persistent right-sided weakness and dysarthria. Post-event CT head demonstrated scattered intracranial air consistent with cerebral arterial gas embolism (paradoxical embolism). Trainees may make two errors: (1) conclude 'the event resolved intra-op, no HBOT needed' — missing that persistent neurologic deficits post-event are the HBOT screening trigger; or (2) read 'venous gas embolism' in the OR note and dismiss it as not the kind of gas embolism HBOT treats — missing the paradoxical spillover into arterial circulation documented on post-event CT. The chart-reading lesson: the criterion is satisfied by documented gas embolism event (intra-op VGE + post-event imaging showing cerebral air), and the persistent neurologic deficits make HBOT screening defensible. Source: NIH PMC5885422 (Verma & Singh — three-case series of VGE during operative hysteroscopy, intra-op recognition pattern, ECHO confirmation, Durant's maneuver management). HBOT trigger pattern extrapolated to paradoxical embolism with persistent CAGE symptoms.

patient.clinical_notes: 33-year-old female presenting for HBOT consultation following an intra-operative cerebral arterial gas embolism event during elective hysteroscopic submucous fibroid resection earlier today (04/14/2026). Patient's history is notable for primary infertility workup and submucous uterine fibroid identified on prior pelvic imaging. Procedure was planned under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation per standard protocol. Approximately 12 minutes into the fibroid resection, the anesthesia team noted a sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 from 36 mmHg to 14 mmHg accompanied by tachycardia, hypotension (BP 88/52), and desaturation to 87%. Chest auscultation revealed a classic millwheel murmur. Surgical team was immediately notified, resection halted, uterine distension fluid released, and the vagina packed with wet gauze. Patient was placed in Durant's maneuver (left lateral tilt with head down position). 100% oxygen administered. Vasopressor support with mephentermine 6mg IV given. Intra-operative transthoracic 2D echocardiogram performed urgently confirmed multiple air bubbles visualized in the right atrium and right ventricle, definitively confirming the diagnosis of venous gas embolism. Air bubbles cleared from cardiac chambers within approximately 12 minutes with supportive measures. Hemodynamics stabilized. Surgery was abandoned. On emergence from anesthesia, patient demonstrated persistent right upper extremity weakness (4/5) and dysarthria, prompting concern for cerebral arterial gas embolism via paradoxical spillover. CT head obtained urgently demonstrated scattered foci of intracranial air in the left MCA distribution and left frontal lobe consistent with cerebral arterial gas embolism. Subsequent MRI brain showed multiple punctate diffusion restriction lesions in the left MCA territory consistent with embolic infarction from gas. Patient transferred to JCMC for hyperbaric oxygen therapy consultation. On arrival, patient remains hemodynamically stable on high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask. Neurologic examination: persistent right upper extremity weakness 4/5, mild dysarthria, cranial nerves otherwise intact, no sensory deficits, alert and oriented. HBOT screening review for emergent recompression therapy.

gas_embolism_documented.evidence: Intra-operative venous gas embolism event documented during hysteroscopic fibroid resection — classic anesthesia crisis with EtCO2 drop (36 → 14 mmHg), millwheel murmur on auscultation, hypotension and desaturation. 2D ECHO confirmed multiple air bubbles in right atrium and right ventricle. Paradoxical embolism to arterial circulation evidenced by persistent post-event neurologic deficits (right hemiparesis + dysarthria) and CT head demonstrating scattered intracranial air in left MCA distribution. MRI brain confirmed embolic infarction pattern from gas.

cases.teaching_moment: The trap on this chart is the intra-operative resolution masking the post-event indication. Trainees who scan the OR note and see 'VGE event resolved with Durant's maneuver + ECHO bubbles cleared in 12 minutes + hemodynamics stabilized' may conclude the event is over and HBOT is unnecessary. That is the wrong call. The criterion is 'Documented gas embolism event' — and the chart documents that event unambiguously: intra-op anesthesia crisis with classic VGE pattern (EtCO2 drop, millwheel murmur, hypotension, desaturation) + 2D ECHO confirming air bubbles in right atrium and right ventricle. The HBOT-defining detail is what happened NEXT: patient emerged from anesthesia with persistent right-sided weakness and dysarthria, and post-event CT head demonstrated scattered intracranial air in the left MCA distribution, with MRI confirming embolic infarction from gas. This is the paradoxical spillover from venous to arterial circulation that creates cerebral arterial gas embolism (CAGE) — and CAGE with persistent neurologic deficits is exactly the clinical scenario for emergent HBOT recompression. The 'venous' label in the OR note describes WHERE the embolism started, not where it ended up. Imaging proves arterial spillover. Lesson: documented gas embolism event + persistent neurologic deficits + imaging evidence of cerebral air = HBOT screening indication, even when the intra-op event itself has resolved. Time-critical: cerebral AGE benefits from HBOT within hours of the event for best neurologic recovery. Do not defer screening because the intra-op crisis was managed successfully.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L3 — Disqualifier teaching case the counterpart to a qualifying gas embolism case. Chart documents a brief air entry event during outpatient hemodialysis (machine air detection alarm triggered, treatment stopped, post-event imaging showing trace venous air in right atrium) BUT patient remained asymptomatic throughout, air self-resolved on observation, no neurologic or cardiac sequelae, no arterial spillover on imaging. HBOT consult was generated reflexively per the dialysis center's air-entry protocol. Trainees who see 'air detected on imaging during dialysis' and immediately reach for GAS_EMBOLISM as the indication miss the chart-reading discriminator: the criterion is 'Documented gas embolism EVENT' — meaning a clinically significant embolism, not just air presence detected somewhere. Asymptomatic incidental venous air with self-resolution does not meet criterion. The chart-reading lesson: gas embolism as an HBOT indication requires the documented event to have clinical consequence — symptoms attributable to the air, imaging evidence of arterial spillover or end-organ effect, or hemodynamic compromise requiring intervention. None of those are present here.

patient.clinical_notes: 71-year-old male with ESRD on chronic hemodialysis (M/W/F schedule) for 4 years, with comorbid Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and CAD status-post CABG 2018, presenting for HBOT consultation following a brief intra-dialytic air entry event earlier today. Patient was undergoing routine outpatient hemodialysis at his usual dialysis center on 05/19/2026 when the dialysis machine's venous line air detector alarm triggered approximately 90 minutes into the treatment session. Per dialysis center staff documentation, the alarm activated as designed, the blood pump stopped automatically, and the venous line was clamped. Estimated volume of air entry was small (less than 5 mL per dialysis nursing assessment). Patient was asymptomatic at the time of the alarm and throughout the subsequent observation period — denied chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness, weakness, headache, visual changes, paresthesia, or any neurologic symptoms. Vital signs remained stable throughout (HR 78 → 82, BP 138/76 → 142/80, SpO2 97% room air, RR 16, afebrile). Patient was placed in left lateral decubitus position per dialysis center protocol and observed for 30 minutes on site. He was then transferred to the local ED for further evaluation. On ED arrival, repeat assessment continued to show patient asymptomatic. Transthoracic 2D echocardiogram demonstrated trace residual air bubbles in the right atrium that resolved spontaneously during the examination, with no air detected in left-sided chambers and no evidence of right-to-left shunt on bubble study. CT head was obtained per ED protocol given the air entry event — completely normal with no intracranial air, no infarct. Chest X-ray showed only baseline cardiomegaly and clear lung fields. Labs unremarkable: troponin negative, D-dimer negative, ABG within expected range for chronic dialysis patient. Patient remained asymptomatic over 4-hour ED observation period. Supplemental oxygen 2 L/min via nasal cannula was started precautionarily on ED arrival but patient maintained adequate saturation on room air throughout. HBOT consultation was generated per the dialysis center's standing air-entry protocol. Patient is hemodynamically stable, neurologically intact, with no symptoms attributable to the air entry event. Screening review for HBOT indication on 05/19/2026.

cases.teaching_moment: This patient does not qualify for HBOT under GAS_EMBOLISM. The criterion is 'Documented gas embolism event' — and the operative word in that criterion is EVENT, meaning a clinically significant embolism with attributable symptoms, hemodynamic consequence, or imaging evidence of end-organ effect. This chart documents air entry (the dialysis machine alarm triggered, trace air was detected on echocardiogram), but it does not document a gas embolism EVENT in the criterion sense. Specifically: (1) patient was asymptomatic at the time of the alarm and throughout subsequent observation — no neurologic, cardiac, pulmonary, or systemic symptoms attributable to the air; (2) imaging confirmed the air was confined to the venous side (right atrium only, no arterial or cerebral spillover on bubble study or CT head); (3) the air self-resolved during the echocardiogram itself — small-volume venous air is cleared physiologically by the pulmonary capillary bed (the liver and lung act as natural bubble traps for small venous gas loads); (4) hemodynamics remained stable throughout, no intervention beyond observation and precautionary positioning was required. The HBOT consultation was generated reflexively per the dialysis center's air-entry protocol, which is a reasonable safety net at the source-facility level but does not by itself establish that the criterion is met. Recommendation: continue current observation, no HBOT indicated, return to dialysis schedule as tolerated, document the event in the patient's record for future reference. Lesson: 'air detected' is not the same as 'gas embolism event.' The criterion requires the event to have clinical consequence — symptoms, hemodynamic compromise, or imaging evidence of arterial spillover or end-organ effect. Asymptomatic incidental venous air with self-resolution is a recognized clinical scenario that does not meet HBOT screening criteria. Do not screen reflexive consults as positive when the chart documents an asymptomatic, self-resolved, venous-only air detection.

cases.teaching_moment: This patient qualifies clearly for HBOT under Gas Gangrene (Clostridial Myonecrosis). The criterion is 'Documented clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene)' — and the chart documents that diagnosis with multiple gold-standard elements aligned: (1) intraoperative tissue culture isolated Clostridium perfringens — the most common clostridial species causing myonecrosis; (2) intraoperative Gram stain demonstrated gram-positive rods with relative paucity of leukocytes — the textbook histopathologic signature called out explicitly in the SHS protocol; (3) CT imaging demonstrated extensive intramuscular gas tracking along fascial planes — the imaging hallmark that distinguishes clostridial myonecrosis from necrotizing fasciitis (intramuscular gas in muscle compartments, not subcutaneous gas in superficial fascia); (4) rapidly progressive tissue destruction documented over 36 hours with bronze-brown discoloration, palpable crepitus, and sweet fetid odor — the classic clinical signature; (5) systemic toxicity documented with fever, leukocytosis, lactate elevation, and vasopressor requirement. The HBO Protocols Manual requires surgical management plus antibiotic therapy as concurrent or prior treatment — both are documented here: initial ED debridement plus emergent radical debridement with fasciotomy, plus triple antibiotic coverage including Clindamycin for its anti-toxin effect against beta-hemolytic clostridial species. HBOT is adjunct to surgical and antibiotic management at 3.0 ATA x 90 minutes, up to 3 treatments in first 24 hours per protocol. Lesson: clostridial myonecrosis is not a subtle screening — when the chart documents tissue culture isolating Clostridium species plus intramuscular gas on imaging plus the classic clinical signature, the audit-defensible documentation chain is complete. Recognize the pattern. Screen confidently. This is time-critical adjunct therapy where delay correlates directly with limb loss and mortality.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L3 — Disqualifier teaching case paired with a qualifying clostridial myonecrosis case to teach the chart-reading discriminator between gas gangrene (qualifies under GAS_GANGRENE) and dry gangrene (does NOT qualify under any HBOT indication). Chart documents dry gangrene of the right great toe and second toe in a 70-year-old male with longstanding diabetes, hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, and tobacco history. The mechanism is chronic arterial occlusion with ischemic mummification — NOT active infection. Arterial Doppler shows no flow distal to mid-calf; CT angiography shows multi-level chronic occlusive disease; cultures show no active infection; no systemic toxicity; no gas on any imaging. The HBOT consult was generated reflexively by the wound care clinic because the diagnosis list contains the word 'gangrene.' Trainees may try to map this to GAS_GANGRENE (criterion fails — no clostridial myonecrosis), DFU (criterion fails — not a Wagner Grade III deep wound with positive radiology or positive deep culture, just dead tissue from chronic ischemia), ACUTE_PAI (criterion fails — mechanism is chronic arterial occlusion, not acute embolus/thrombus), or COMPROMISED_GRAFT (criterion fails — no graft). The audit-defensible answer is DOES_NOT_QUALIFY — patient needs vascular surgery evaluation for revascularization workup or amputation planning, not HBOT. Source: NIH PMC6891997 (clinical features section — dry gangrene definition, mechanism, comorbidity profile, imaging documentation pattern) + standard SHS screening rationale for dry gangrene as non-HBOT-indication.

cases.teaching_moment: This patient does not qualify for HBOT under any indication. The diagnosis is dry gangrene from chronic peripheral arterial occlusive disease — ischemic mummification of distal tissue due to gradual loss of arterial inflow. This is a DIFFERENT clinical entity from gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis), and the chart documents the distinction explicitly. Chart-reading proof of the mechanism: arterial Doppler shows multi-level chronic occlusive disease with no measurable arterial flow distal to mid-calf; CT angiography confirms severe multi-level chronic PAD with right SFA occlusion and poor collateral reconstitution; toe pressure is 12 mmHg (severely reduced); the tissue is dry, mummified, and well-demarcated with no active infection. Chart-reading proof of what this is NOT: CT angiography explicitly documents no gas in soft tissues; X-ray confirms no subcutaneous or intramuscular gas, no abscess, no osteomyelitis; superficial wound culture shows no growth; WBC is normal at 7,400; lactate is normal at 1.4; patient is afebrile with no systemic toxicity. Now walk through the indication mapping: (1) NOT GAS_GANGRENE — criterion requires documented clostridial myonecrosis; this chart has no clostridial isolation, no gas on imaging, no surgical debridement of active infection, no systemic toxicity. The chart actively documents the absence of these features. (2) NOT DFU — criterion requires Wagner Grade III or higher (deep wound with positive radiology for osteomyelitis or positive deep wound culture showing moderate-to-heavy growth); this is ischemic mummification, not a stageable wound. (3) NOT ACUTE_PAI — criterion requires acute onset of ischemia 2nd to arterial embolus or thrombus; this is chronic occlusive disease over years. (4) NOT COMPROMISED_GRAFT — applies to recent grafts/flaps at risk of failure, not to chronic occluded bypass grafts from 2022. The correct answer is DOES_NOT_QUALIFY. Recommended pathway: vascular surgery evaluation for revascularization workup, transmetatarsal amputation planning, or supervised autoamputation depending on revascularization candidacy. Lesson: 'gangrene' is not one diagnosis — it is a descriptive term covering multiple distinct clinical entities with different mechanisms and different treatment pathways. Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is an HBOT indication. Dry gangrene by itself — from chronic arterial occlusion, without other qualifying clinical features — is not a covered HBOT indication. The chart-reading skill is recognizing the mechanism documentation and matching it to the correct indication, not pattern-matching on the word in the diagnosis list.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L3 — Diabetic foot wound disqualifier that fails the Wagner Grade III screening criterion despite clinical features that pattern-match DFU on surface read. Chart documents a full-thickness wound on the dorsal aspect of the right foot with extensor tendon visible, surrounding cellulitis, undermining 12-6 o'clock, and significant necrotic tissue — visually presenting as a severe DFU. However, the objective evidence required to establish Wagner Grade III FAILS the criterion: X-ray NEGATIVE for osteomyelitis, MRI NEGATIVE for osteomyelitis, deep wound cultures NEGATIVE for infection. Wagner Grade III per the SHS DFU criterion requires a deep wound PLUS either positive radiology for osteomyelitis OR positive deep wound culture showing moderate-to-heavy growth. This patient has the deep wound but neither positive imaging nor positive culture. Trainees who see 'deep wound + tendon exposed + necrotic tissue + diabetic + cellulitis' may reflexively map to Wagner Grade III without checking whether the audit-defensible documentation actually supports it. The lesson: Wagner Grade III is not established by visual severity, it is established by the documentation chain (deep wound + positive imaging OR positive culture). When both imaging modalities AND cultures are explicitly negative, the criterion fails. Patient was successfully treated with advanced wound care alone (healed in 8 weeks) — proving the screening decision matches clinical reality.

cases.teaching_moment: This patient does not qualify for HBOT under any indication. The chart pattern-matches DFU on surface read (diabetic patient + full-thickness foot wound + necrotic tissue + visible extensor tendon + surrounding cellulitis + classic high-risk comorbidity stack), but the audit-defensible Wagner Grade III documentation FAILS. The SHS DFU criterion for Wagner Grade III reads 'Deep wound with either Positive Radiology Results or Positive Culture' — and this chart documents the deep wound but explicitly fails BOTH the radiology and culture pathways. X-ray right foot on 03/02/2026: NO osteomyelitis, NO subcutaneous gas, NO abscess. MRI right foot with and without contrast on 03/09/2026: NO osteomyelitis on T1, T2, or post-contrast sequences, NO deep abscess, NO joint involvement. Deep wound culture on 03/09/2026: NO growth, no infection identified. Repeat wound swab on 03/16/2026: only light skin flora, no significant pathogens. Now walk the indication mapping: (1) NOT DFU — Wagner Grade III criterion requires deep wound PLUS positive radiology OR positive culture. Both pathways explicitly negative on this chart. (2) NOT ACUTE_PAI — patient has chronic PVD with reduced ABI 0.78 on the affected side, but the criterion requires acute onset of ischemia 2nd to arterial embolus or thrombus. This is chronic occlusive disease, not acute event. (3) NOT CROM — no documented prior osteomyelitis in the same location, no current osteomyelitis on imaging. (4) NOT NEC_FASC — no purulence, no odor, no crepitation, no rapid progression, no polymicrobial culture, no systemic toxicity. Correct answer is DOES_NOT_QUALIFY. Recommended pathway: continue advanced wound care management with serial debridement, dressing optimization, vascular reassessment if wound stalls, and infection surveillance if clinical picture changes. Lesson: Wagner Grade III is not established by visual severity of the wound. It is established by the documentation chain — deep wound PLUS positive imaging OR positive culture. When both pathways are explicitly negative, the criterion fails regardless of how severe the wound appears on examination. This patient was successfully treated with advanced wound care alone (healed in 8 weeks) — proving that the screening decision matches clinical reality. cases.difficulty_explanation: L3 — Disqualifier teaching case (45M Thanksgiving turkey fryer spill → right lower leg deep second-degree thermal burn, healed in 11 days with advanced wound care alone — NO HBOT). The HBOT consult was generated because the wound center sees 'extensive deep burn + necrotic tissue + significant debridement needed' and trainees may know from broader UHMS literature exposure that HBOT is used for burns at some centers. The chart-reading lesson: CMS NCD 20.29(B) explicitly lists 'Skin burns (thermal)' as item #4 on the Noncovered Conditions list. This is a categorical federal Medicare coverage exclusion, not a documentation gap or a SHS scope choice. The audit-defensible answer is DOES_NOT_QUALIFY regardless of wound severity, regardless of clinical appearance, regardless of UHMS broader guidance about burn benefit at some centers. The screening trainee must distinguish 'clinical might-help' from 'CMS coverage policy.' Source: CMS National Coverage Determination 20.29 (covered + noncovered conditions list).

cases.teaching_moment: This patient does not qualify for HBOT under any CMS indication, but may qualify under a third party payor insurance plan. The diagnosis is definitively established: deep second-degree thermal burn from a turkey fryer spill on 11/27/2025, presenting 3 days post-injury. The screening answer here is grounded in federal Medicare coverage policy. CMS National Coverage Determination 20.29(B) — the Noncovered Conditions list — explicitly identifies 'Skin burns (thermal)' as item #4 in its enumeration of conditions that Medicare does not cover under HBOT. This is a categorical coverage exclusion at the federal policy level, NOT a documentation gap. No additional workup, no more imaging, no repeat cultures, and no additional clinical detail would change the screening outcome for a Medicare covered individual. Thermal burns are simply not covered by Medicare for HBOT. Now walk the indication map to confirm no other covered indication fits: (1) NOT GAS_GANGRENE — criterion requires documented clostridial myonecrosis. This chart has no clostridial culture, no intramuscular gas, no systemic toxicity, no operative debridement for active infection. (2) NOT NEC_FASC — criterion requires documented progressive necrotizing infection used as adjunct to aggressive surgical debridement plus antibiotics. The necrotic tissue here is burn-related necrosis with stable margins, not a progressive necrotizing infectious process. (3) NOT COMPROMISED_GRAFT — no graft was placed. (4) NOT CRUSH_INJURY or ACUTE_TRAUMATIC_PI — no traumatic mechanism causing threatened limb ischemia. The audit-defensible answer is DOES_NOT_QUALIFY. Recommended pathway: continue advanced wound care management with Aquacel Ag and bi-weekly dressing changes per the current plan. Note: thermal burns CAN escalate to indication-meeting status if complications develop — clostridial superinfection (would screen as GAS_GANGRENE), invasive necrotizing infection (would screen as NEC_FASC), or surgical skin grafting with compromised graft viability (would screen as COMPROMISED_GRAFT). None of those complications are documented at this presentation. Lesson: the screening question is grounded in CMS coverage policy, not clinical 'might HBOT help.' UHMS broader clinical guidance about burn benefit at some centers does NOT override CMS NCD coverage exclusions. When CMS explicitly noncovers a condition in NCD 20.29(B), screening returns DOES_NOT_QUALIFY regardless of wound severity or clinical appearance. This patient healed in 11 days across 5 visits with advanced wound care alone, no HBOT required.

patient.clinical_notes: 60-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes, obesity (BMI 38), hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease, presenting for HBOT consultation following surgical management of Fournier's gangrene. Initial presentation began on 01/03/2026 with a perirectal abscess that was managed with bedside incision and drainage at the local emergency department. Over the subsequent 4-5 days, patient developed progressively worsening pain, erythema, and necrotic changes extending from the perirectal region into the buttocks, perineum, scrotum, and lower abdominal wall, prompting transfer to a tertiary care center on 01/08/2026 for emergent evaluation. On admission, patient was septic with WBC 26,400, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, CRP 31.2 mg/dL, and required low-dose norepinephrine support for hemodynamic stability. CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast demonstrated extensive subcutaneous gas tracking through perineum, scrotum, bilateral buttocks, and lower abdominal wall consistent with progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection — radiologic diagnosis of Fournier's gangrene. Patient was taken emergently to the operating room for radical surgical debridement of all affected areas, with creation of a diverting loop colostomy for fecal stream diversion to protect the perineal wound bed during healing (standard Fournier's gangrene management). Wide-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated immediately with Piperacillin-Tazobactam, Vancomycin, and Clindamycin (the latter for its antitoxin effect against beta-hemolytic streptococcal species). Intraoperative cultures grew polymicrobial flora consistent with Fournier's gangrene — Streptococcus species plus Bacteroides plus Escherichia coli plus mixed anaerobes. Tissue Gram stain showed polymicrobial flora with extensive inflammatory cells and necrotic debris. Patient was discharged from the acute surgical service on hospital day 10 after stabilization and started HBOT the following day (01/19/2026) as adjunct to ongoing surgical and antibiotic management per established Fournier's gangrene treatment protocol. On HBOT day 2, VAC was placed at 175 mmHg continuous with a single layer of Acticoat Burn underlay for the first four dressing changes. HBOT protocol planned at 2.0 ATA × 120 minutes per session, with bi-weekly dressing changes between sessions. Patient is hemodynamically stable at HBOT consultation, alert and oriented despite illness severity, neurologically intact, on low-dose vasopressor support being weaned. Screening review on 01/19/2026 for HBOT continuation as adjunct to surgical and antibiotic management.
