cases.teaching_moment: This patient qualifies clearly for HBOT under NEC_FASC (Progressive Necrotizing Infection). Fournier's gangrene is a recognized anatomically-specific subtype of necrotizing fasciitis involving the perineum, genitalia, and adjacent regions — it is the same indication as more familiar extremity or abdominal nec fasc presentations, just in a different anatomical territory. The criteria are both satisfied: (1) Documented progressive necrotizing infection — chart documents the precipitating perirectal abscess (01/03/2026 with I&D), rapidly progressive necrotic changes over 4-5 days extending across multiple anatomical regions, CT confirming extensive subcutaneous gas tracking through perineum/scrotum/buttocks/lower abdomen consistent with progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection, intraoperative polymicrobial cultures showing the typical Fournier's flora (Streptococcus + Bacteroides + E. coli + anaerobes), severe leukocytosis (WBC 26,400), elevated lactate (3.8), elevated CRP (31.2), and sepsis with vasopressor requirement. (2) Used as adjunct to aggressive surgical debridement and antibiotic therapy — chart documents radical surgical debridement of all affected areas on 01/08/2026 with creation of a diverting loop colostomy for fecal stream diversion (standard Fournier's management to protect the perineal wound bed during healing), plus wide-spectrum IV antibiotic therapy with Piperacillin-Tazobactam plus Vancomycin plus Clindamycin (the latter specifically added for its antitoxin effect against beta-hemolytic streptococcal species). HBOT was initiated 01/19/2026 as adjunct to ongoing surgical and antibiotic management. Note the differential from GAS_GANGRENE: this is necrotizing fasciitis (subcutaneous and fascial involvement) with polymicrobial culture — NOT clostridial myonecrosis (which would require isolated clostridial species on culture and intramuscular gas in muscle compartments). The chart-reading discriminator is microbiology (polymicrobial vs clostridial-specific) and anatomy (subcutaneous/fascial vs intramuscular gas distribution). Lesson: Fournier's gangrene is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia — recognize the anatomical subtype, screen confidently under NEC_FASC. The chart documents the polymicrobial Fournier's flora, the radical surgical management with diverting ostomy, and the wide-spectrum antibiotic therapy that establish HBOT as the adjunct therapy per protocol. This is the textbook clinical scenario where HBOT adjunct therapy is associated with improved outcomes.

cases.difficulty_explanation: L5 — Patient presents with an extraordinary CROM-pattern documentation package: two prior episodes of osteomyelitis at the same anatomical location, two 6-week IV Vancomycin courses, two surgical debridements, persistent MRSA on repeat bone biopsy, surveillance MRI showing refractory osteomyelitis unchanged from pre-treatment imaging. The reflexive read is CROM — the chart 'looks like CROM' on every detail. The L5 chart-reading work is recognizing that this is NOT primarily a CROM case for HBOT screening purposes — it is a diabetic foot ulcer at Wagner Grade III with the osteomyelitis serving as the Wagner III qualifier, all standard DFU criteria documented over a ~5 month window (07/2025 recurrence → 12/2025 screening), including 30 days of standard wound care with no measurable healing. The osteomyelitis-on-imaging satisfies the Wagner Grade III requirement for DFU pathway (deep wound with positive radiology) — the osteo IS the qualifier for DFU, not a separate indication pulling the case toward CROM. CROM as a standalone HBOT indication is more commonly used when osteomyelitis presents WITHOUT a current open wound (post-surgical sternal, mandibular, vertebral) or in non-diabetic patients. For a diabetic patient with a current open lower-extremity wound + underlying osteomyelitis + all standard DFU workup elements documented over 30+ days, the audit-defensible primary indication is DFU. Source: SHS HBO Protocols Manual (Diabetic Wounds + Chronic Refractory Osteomyelitis side-by-side comparison) + CMS NCD 20.29(A)(15) (DFU) and (A)(10) (CROM). This case teaches the principle that osteomyelitis in a diabetic foot ulcer is the Wagner III qualifier, NOT necessarily a separate CROM indication — and that elaborate osteo-specific treatment documentation does not automatically pull a diabetic-foot-wound case into the CROM pathway.

patient.clinical_notes: 69-year-old male with 18-year history of Type 2 diabetes, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, mild peripheral arterial disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, presenting for HBOT consultation for chronic refractory osteomyelitis of the right great toe distal phalanx. FIRST EPISODE: In August 2023, patient developed a diabetic foot ulcer at the right great toe that progressed to osteomyelitis confirmed on MRI 08/01/2023 (bone marrow edema, cortical erosion, marrow signal abnormality consistent with active osteomyelitis right great toe distal phalanx). Patient underwent surgical debridement on 08/14/2023 followed by a 6-week course of IV Vancomycin via PICC line. Follow-up MRI on 02/12/2024 demonstrated resolution of osteomyelitis findings with only post-debridement changes — first episode resolved. Patient remained ulcer-free and infection-free for approximately 17 months with appropriate diabetic foot care including diabetic shoes with custom inserts, off-loading, and routine foot surveillance. SECOND EPISODE: In July 2025, patient noted recurrent ulceration at the SAME anatomical location (right great toe distal phalanx). MRI on 07/14/2025 confirmed recurrent osteomyelitis at the same site as the 2023 episode. Bone biopsy on 07/22/2025 was again positive for MRSA with the same susceptibility profile. Infectious Disease has documented failure of conventional surgical + medical management of the osteomyelitis. cases.teaching_moment: This is the flipped switcharoo: a diabetic patient with a foot wound and underlying osteomyelitis can theoretically be screened under DFU OR CROM, but the audit-defensible chart-reading work identifies DFU as the correct primary indication for this specific patient. The discriminator is the clinical scenario shape: this is a current open lower-extremity wound in a diabetic patient with osteomyelitis on imaging — that is a Wagner Grade III DFU by definition. The osteomyelitis is the Wagner III qualifier (deep wound with positive radiology), not a separate indication pulling the case toward CROM. Walk through the DFU criteria carefully: (1) Diabetes — yes, T2DM 18 years on insulin + metformin with documented neuropathy. (2) Wagner Grade III or higher — yes, wound at right great toe (lower extremity) with osteomyelitis confirmed on MRI 07/14/2025 and surveillance MRI 12/05/2025. Deep wound + positive radiology = Wagner III. (3) 30 days of standard wound care — yes, 07/2025 recurrence through 12/2025 screening is ~5 months of continuous SWC. (4) No measurable healing — yes, wound measurements 11/15/2025 (1.9 x 1.3 x 0.5) → 12/15/2025 (1.8 x 1.2 x 0.5) show minimal change. (5) Debridements documented — yes, 08/14/2023 + 07/22/2025. (6) Off-loading — yes, diabetic shoes + custom inserts + cane. (7) Glucose control — yes, HbA1c 7.6 on insulin + metformin. (8) Vascular assessment — yes, ABI 0.74 documented 11/20/2025. (9) Nutritional assessment — yes, albumin 3.4 + pre-albumin 16. (10) Moist dressings — yes, calcium alginate daily. (11) Infection treatment — yes, IV Vancomycin + surgical debridements. All 11 DFU criteria documented. CROM as a standalone HBOT indication is more commonly the pathway when osteomyelitis presents WITHOUT a current open wound (post-surgical sternal, mandibular, vertebral) or in non-diabetic patients. For a diabetic patient with a current open lower-extremity wound + underlying osteomyelitis + all standard DFU workup documented, the audit-defensible primary indication is DFU. The osteomyelitis-on-imaging satisfies Wagner Grade III; it does not require a separate CROM screening pathway. Lesson: when a diabetic patient with foot involvement and underlying osteomyelitis presents for HBOT screening, do not let elaborate CROM-pattern documentation pull you off the DFU pathway. The clinical scenario shape — current open lower-extremity wound in a diabetic patient with osteo-on-imaging — IS a DFU at Wagner Grade III. The L5 chart-reading skill here is recognizing that 'osteo in a diabetic foot ulcer' is the Wagner III qualifier, not a separate indication.
